answer.exemplar: A converging lens refracts light, and the amount it refracts depends on the refractive index, which for glass is not the same at every wavelength. The index is larger for the shorter violet wavelengths than for the longer red ones, so the lens is a slightly stronger lens for violet and brings it to a focus nearer the lens than it brings red. Because no single image plane suits both, the colours cannot all meet at the point where the average focus lies, and a small ring of colour survives: violet at the inner edge and red at the outer edge, matching what is observed. Nothing in the lens alters any frequency, so the colours that emerge are the colours that entered, and the defect is small for a thin lens of small aperture and grows as either increases, which is why cheap lenses show a coloured edge under strong light.

questions.explanation: The lens bends light in proportion to how strongly the medium slows it, and the index of glass varies with wavelength, being larger for violet than for red. The lens is therefore a slightly stronger lens for violet than for red, so its focal length is a little shorter for violet, and the two colours cross the axis at different distances, violet first. The extreme colours focus furthest apart, so no single plane brings them together and a small coloured ring survives at the best focus, with red at the outer edge on the short-wavelength side of the spread. A good answer would also note that no frequency is changed, so the colours are the same colours that entered, and that the effect is small for a thin lens and grows with the amount of glass and the aperture.

answer.exemplar: Two slits produce a stationary pattern only if the phase relationship between the light arriving at them is fixed in time, because the brightness at each point of the screen is set by a difference of path lengths that is itself constant. A single narrow source guarantees this: both slits are illuminated by the same wavefront, so the extra path one slit receives from any particular part of the source is unchanging, and the same fringes reappear on every repetition. A broad lamp emits from many independent regions with unrelated phases, so the extra path from each region keeps changing and the interference contributions at any point sum to the average intensity, giving a uniform blur. A single slit or a narrow filter in front of the broad lamp restores the fixed phase relationship and the pattern returns.

questions.explanation: A stable pattern exists only if the interference term averages to the same value at every moment and at every repetition of the pattern. That requires a fixed relationship in phase between the light reaching the two slits, which is what a single narrow source guarantees because both slits see the same wavefront and any path difference between them is constant in time. With a broad lamp the two slits receive light from many independent emitting regions whose relative phases jump unpredictably, so the interference term cancels on average and only the summed intensities survive, which is a uniform blur. A good answer would also connect this to a single slit or a narrow filter, since narrowing the source is exactly what restores the phase relationship.

answer.exemplar: A wave of one frequency repeats identically for ever, with every cycle the same, so it has no beginning and no end and cannot describe a pulse a few cycles long. A short pulse must therefore be a superposition of a spread of frequencies, with their phases arranged so that they add up over the short interval occupied by the pulse and very nearly cancel everywhere outside it. As the pulse travels, those component frequencies do not all keep their relative phases, because on a stretched string the wave speed depends on wavelength and each component has a different one, so their spacing drifts. The reinforcement at the front and the cancellation at the tails are then no longer exact: the edges round off, the peak spreads out and drops, and the pulse arrives weaker and broader however far it has gone.

questions.explanation: A single frequency describes a wave that repeats forever, with every cycle identical, so it can never be a pulse that begins and ends. A short pulse must instead be built from a spread of frequencies whose phases are arranged so that they reinforce over the short interval of the pulse and very nearly cancel outside it, which is the superposition principle applied in reverse. A good answer will also say what travel does to the shape: the different frequencies travel at different speeds along a stretched string, so their relative phases drift as the pulse moves, the sharp edges soften and the peak spreads and falls, so a pulse never arrives unchanged however far it goes.
